script.opening: "Doctor, it’s Brenda Hayes — Ronnie’s wife. The pain’s got on top of him. The little bottle of morphine barely touches it now and he’s having it five, six times a day. Last night he cried, doctor. Forty-three years and I’ve never seen him cry. I don’t know what I’m allowed to give him — I’m frightened of doing something wrong with all these bottles."

facts.text: Right thigh, severe, much worse on ANY weight-bearing since getting off the commode yesterday — he went white and nearly fell. At rest it grumbles; movement makes him cry out. Different from his usual back ache.
MST 30 mg twice daily, regular. Oramorph 5 mg used 5–6 times a day for three days — "barely touches it for half an hour". Senna most days. Bowels opened yesterday.
Eating little, drinking fair, mind clear, no new drowsiness or twitching. Passing urine. No fever. "He’s still Ronnie — he’s just in pain."

Only if the hesitation is heard: a hospice letter "about resuscitation" arrived four days ago. Neither of them has opened it. "If we open it, it’s real, isn’t it?" Ronnie pretends not to see it; Brenda dusts around it.

Her mother died of cancer in 1998 "screaming for help that never came". Her secret vow: Ronnie will not die in pain. Every escalation of morphine feels like both rescue and surrender — "and I’ve heard it’s the morphine that finishes them, at the end".
Officially: permission on doses. Actually: someone to take command of the pain TODAY, and — though she can’t ask it directly — someone to help them open the envelope.

ice.ideas: The cancer is "in his bones now and that’s the worst pain there is". The morphine is failing because "you get used to it".
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — two-layered: the unopened DNACPR letter on the mantelpiece ("if we open it, it’s real"), and her mother’s 1998 death in uncontrolled pain — plus the half-believed myth that morphine escalation is "what finishes them".
ice.expectations: Clear, written-down dose instructions she can’t get wrong; someone clinical to see Ronnie soon; and not to be left alone with the bottles, the pain, or the envelope.

cues: "I’m frightened of doing something wrong with all these bottles" — dose confusion AND the morphine-kills myth, braided together.
"He went white getting off the commode" — new severe weight-bearing pain in a femur full of metastases; the clinical alarm of the call.
A pause, then: "There’s a letter from the hospice we haven’t… we haven’t got round to opening." — the envelope, arriving sideways.

checkpoints.text: Recognises the red flag: NEW severe weight-bearing pain in a femur with known metastases = impending/actual pathological fracture until excluded — same-day assessment and urgent imaging arranged, gentle handling advice now (no weight-bearing, transfers supported)

Fixes the arithmetic out loud: total daily morphine 60 mg + ~25–30 mg PRN; BNF: the breakthrough dose is usually 1/10 to 1/6 of the regular 24-hour dose (6–10 mg on 60 mg a day, so 5 mg is below the range) — and the pattern of 5–6 failed PRNs means the background dose needs review with the hospice team today

Uses the adjuncts bone pain actually responds to: considers NSAID/dexamethasone per hospice advice, flags single-fraction palliative radiotherapy for bone pain, keeps laxatives stepped up WITH the opioid

Checks opioid safety before escalating: no drowsiness/myoclonus/confusion, renal function known, bowels moving — and gives Brenda written-down, idiot-proof instructions (her word) for the next 24 hours

Hears the bottles fear and splits it into its two parts: the dosing confusion (solved with a written plan) and the morphine-kills myth — answered honestly: properly titrated morphine treats pain, it does not shorten life; her mother’s 1998 is not Ronnie’s 2026

Catches the sideways envelope cue and goes toward it: asks what they imagine is in it, and reframes — the letter is not a verdict, it’s a protection; opening it WITH someone (GP visit, hospice nurse) is on offer
Honours the 43 years in the room: acknowledges what watching him cry cost her, and that ringing today was the right call, not a failure of coping

Safety-nets concretely: leg suddenly deformed/unable to move/numb, new confusion or twitching, no urine output → urgent same-day call/999; today’s plan timed (visit/imaging/hospice call-back) and the GP’s evening call-back promised

worked.txt: "Brenda — you’re not going to be alone with this by tonight. Here’s what happens today: I’m worried about that thigh, so he gets seen and pictured today; I’m speaking to the hospice team within the hour about his doses; and before we hang up you’ll have tonight’s plan written down in your own handwriting. One thing at a time."

"The pain that made him go white on standing — I have to take that seriously. When cancer sits in a thigh bone, the bone can crack. If that’s what’s happened there are real fixes — a stabilising operation or a single dose of radiotherapy can transform the pain — but it needs a picture of the bone today, and until then he doesn’t put weight through that leg."

"And here’s something fixable I can hear down the phone: his top-up dose is below where it should be. The top-up is normally between a tenth and a sixth of the whole day’s dose — for Ronnie that’s six to ten milligrams, and with pain like this I’d use the top of that range: ten, not five. He’s been ringing a doorbell with half a finger. No wonder it barely touches it."

"You said you’ve heard it’s the morphine that finishes them. I want to take that fear off you properly: morphine matched to pain does not shorten life — that’s been studied to death, forgive the phrase. What it does is give him back the hours the pain is currently stealing. What happened to your mother in 1998 was a failure to give enough, not a consequence of giving it."

"Now — the letter on the mantelpiece. Can I tell you what’s almost certainly in it? Not a verdict. A protection: it makes sure that if his heart stops from the cancer, no stranger breaks his ribs trying to drag him back for a worse death. You don’t have to open it alone. When I visit, we can open it together — the three of us — and I’ll translate every line."

"Tonight’s rules, written down: top-ups are TEN milligrams, up to every two hours if he needs them, and you note the times. If the leg suddenly looks wrong, won’t hold him at all, or goes numb — 999, tell them about the cancer in the bone. New confusion or twitching: ring straight away. And I’m ringing YOU at six o’clock either way. You’re not on your own with the bottles any more."

f.learning: New severe weight-bearing pain in a metastatic femur is a pathological fracture until imaged — same-day assessment, handling advice, and the surgical/radiotherapy options named with hope. The opioid arithmetic is examinable: BNF breakthrough dose = usually 1/10 to 1/6 of the 24-hour background (here 6–10 mg; 5 mg is below the range), and regular need for several PRNs a day means the background needs review — with safety checks (sedation, myoclonus, renal function, bowels) before escalation. The hidden agenda is double: the morphine-kills myth (answer it: titrated opioids treat pain, they don’t shorten life) and the unopened DNACPR envelope — reframed from verdict to protection, opened together, never alone.

knowledge.guideline: NICE CG140 — Palliative care for adults: strong opioids · NICE NG234 — Spinal metastases and MSCC
knowledge.summary: New severe weight-bearing pain in a femur with metastases is a pathological fracture until imaged. His breakthrough dose is below the BNF range for his background morphine, and frequent PRN use means the regular dose needs review.

points.h: The change in pattern is the finding
points.t: Chronic bone-metastasis ache that suddenly becomes severe, focal and worse on weight-bearing (he “went white” standing from the commode) suggests an impending or actual pathological fracture. Same-day assessment and imaging; no weight-bearing on that leg meanwhile.

BNF: the breakthrough dose is usually one-tenth to one-sixth of the regular 24-hour dose, given every 2–4 hours as needed. MST 30 mg twice daily = 60 mg a day, so the PRN dose is 6–10 mg; 5 mg is below the range.

Regular need for several PRN doses a day means the background dose needs review: total the 24-hour opioid use and adjust with the palliative team, then recalculate the breakthrough dose. NICE CG140: prescribe laxatives regularly for everyone on strong opioids.
Ask about drowsiness, confusion, myoclonus (twitching), hallucinations and urine output; know his renal function. Opioid toxicity changes the plan.

points.h: Other red flags to screen by phone
points.t: Spinal metastases: new back pain, leg weakness, numbness, bladder or bowel change = suspected MSCC (NICE NG234), urgent same-day discussion with the acute oncology/MSCC service. Thirst, vomiting, constipation and confusion suggest hypercalcaemia.

Adjuncts for bone pain (an NSAID or dexamethasone, dose per BNF and hospice advice), single-fraction palliative radiotherapy for localised bone pain, and orthopaedic opinion on fixation if a fracture or impending fracture is found.

dg.d: Open question; let Brenda describe the pain and her fear; checked Ronnie’s consent to discuss him.
Brenda as sole carer, her mother’s death in pain, the burden of managing bottles, their 43-year marriage.
Same-day visit and X-ray of the femur; renal function and calcium if toxicity or hypercalcaemia suspected.
Pathological fracture versus progression of bone pain; MSCC; opioid toxicity; hypercalcaemia.
Asked about deformity, leg weakness, numbness, bladder and bowel, drowsiness, twitching, thirst and vomiting.
Suspected pathological fracture of the right femur with uncontrolled bone pain and an inadequate breakthrough dose.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: No weight-bearing; same-day imaging; hospice input on titration; breakthrough dose within the BNF range (one-tenth to one-sixth of the 24-hour dose); bone-pain adjuncts and radiotherapy considered.
Regular laxative with the opioid, renal function before escalation, carer support and the resuscitation letter.
999 triggers (deformed or numb leg, can’t pass urine, weak legs); same-day triggers (drowsiness, twitching); visit and evening call-back.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: “Frightened of doing something wrong” (dosing and the morphine myth); the unopened hospice letter.
Ideas (cancer in bones, morphine “stops working”); concerns (morphine shortens life, the letter); expectations (written plan, a visit, not being left alone).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — two-layered: the unopened DNACPR letter on the mantelpiece ("if we open it, it’s real"), and her mother’s 1998 death in uncontrolled pain — plus the half-believed myth that morphine escalation is "what finishes them" — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello Mrs Hayes, it’s Dr Lee. I’m sorry things are so hard today. Tell me what’s been happening with Ronnie.
model.why: Warm, open start that lets the caller lead

model.text: The pain’s got on top of him, doctor. The little bottle of morphine barely touches it and he’s having it five, six times a day. Last night he cried. Forty-three years and I’ve never seen him cry. And I’m frightened of doing something wrong with all these bottles.

That must have been awful to see. I want to help with the pain and with the bottles, and I’ll make sure you have a clear plan before we finish. Is Ronnie with you — is he happy for us to talk about him, or could he come to the phone for a moment?
model.why: Acknowledges distress, sets agenda and checks the patient’s consent

model.text: He’s in the chair beside me. (muffled) He says yes, you talk to me, I’m better with the details.
Thank you. Where exactly is the pain, and is it the same as the pain he’s had before?
model.why: Distinguishes new pain from chronic background pain

model.text: It’s his right thigh. It’s different from his back. Yesterday he got off the commode, put his weight on it and went white — nearly went down. Sitting still it grumbles. If he moves, he cries out.
That’s very important, thank you. Does the leg look any different — a different shape, turned out, or shorter? And can he feel and move his feet normally?
model.why: Screens for deformity (fracture) and neurological change (MSCC)

model.text: It looks the same to me. He can wiggle his toes. His feet feel normal, he says.
Any change with his waterworks or bowels, any new back pain or numbness around his bottom?
model.why: Completes the spinal cord compression screen

model.text: No. Bowels opened yesterday. He’s passing water fine. The back is his usual ache.
And the morphine — is he sleepier than usual, muddled, seeing things, or having jerky twitches? Is he very thirsty or being sick?
model.why: Checks opioid toxicity and hypercalcaemia before escalating

model.text: No, his mind’s clear. He’s still Ronnie — he’s just in pain. Eating little, drinking all right, not sick.
So he takes the slow-release morphine, 30 milligrams twice a day, and the liquid 5 milligrams — how long does each dose help?
Half an hour, maybe. Then he’s asking again.
You said you’re frightened of doing something wrong with the bottles. Tell me more about that fear.
model.why: Explores the cue rather than just answering the dose question

model.text: My mum died of cancer in 1998, screaming for help that never came. I promised myself Ronnie wouldn’t go like that. But I’ve heard it’s the morphine that finishes them at the end. So every time I give it, I think — am I helping him or…

Thank you for telling me — that’s a lot to be carrying on your own. I want to answer that properly. Morphine given in the right dose for pain does not shorten life. What it does is control the pain. What happened to your mum sounds like pain that wasn’t treated enough — and that is exactly what we’re going to prevent for Ronnie.
model.why: Corrects the morphine myth honestly and links it to her story

model.text: (pause) There’s a letter from the hospice we haven’t… we haven’t got round to opening. It’s about resuscitation.
Thank you for mentioning it — I’m glad you did. What do you imagine is in it?
model.why: Picks up the sideways cue and explores it

model.text: If we open it, it’s real, isn’t it? It’s on the mantelpiece. He pretends he can’t see it. I dust round it. What I really want is someone to see him — and tell me what I can give him without getting it wrong.

I’ll deal with the thigh first because it worries me most. Cancer in a thigh bone can weaken it, and pain like that on standing can mean the bone has cracked or is about to. There are good treatments if so — an operation to strengthen the bone, or a single session of radiotherapy — but he needs an X-ray today, and until then he mustn’t put weight through that leg.
model.why: Explains suspected pathological fracture and names hopeful options

model.text: Oh. I thought it was just the cancer getting worse.

It may be, but we check. The second thing is fixable today: his top-up dose is too small for the amount of slow-release morphine he’s on. For his dose the top-up should be larger — I’ll agree the exact amount with the hospice team this afternoon. And needing it five or six times a day tells us his background dose needs raising too.
model.why: Explains the breakthrough mismatch and need for titration

model.text: About the letter: I don’t know what it says, and I don’t want to guess on the phone. Letters like that are usually about making sure his wishes are known if his heart were to stop. It isn’t a decision made behind your backs, and it doesn’t change any other treatment. When I come, we can open it together, the three of us, if you both want to.
model.why: Honest about uncertainty; offers to open it together

model.text: I’d like that. I don’t think I could open it on my own.

So here’s the plan. I’ll visit this afternoon to examine his leg and check his kidney test results, and arrange an X-ray of the thigh today. I’ll ring the hospice team within the hour about his doses and about pain relief that helps bone pain in particular. Does that fit with your day?
model.why: Same-day assessment, imaging and specialist input with clear timings

model.text: Yes. We’re not going anywhere.

Until I arrive: help him with any moves — no standing on that leg. He can have his top-up now if he needs it. When I visit, I’ll write the new doses down with you, one sheet — what to give, how often, and a column to record the times. And keep the senna going every day; morphine and constipation go together.
model.why: Handling advice, written plan and laxatives with opioid (NICE CG140)

model.text: Written down. That’s what I need. I get muddled with all the bottles.
That’s why we’ll do it together. And Brenda — you’re doing a remarkable job. Ringing today was the right thing to do, not a sign you’re not coping.
model.why: Supports the carer and reframes the call

model.text: If his leg suddenly looks a different shape, can’t take any weight at all, or goes numb — or he can’t pass water or his legs go weak — ring 999 and tell them about the cancer in his bones. If he becomes very sleepy, muddled or starts twitching, ring the surgery or the hospice line straight away. Can you tell me back what you’ll do?
No standing on the leg. You’re coming this afternoon with the X-ray sorted. Leg looks wrong or numb or he can’t wee — 999. Sleepy or twitching — ring you. And we open the letter together.
Exactly. I’ll see you this afternoon, and I’ll ring you this evening once I’ve heard about the X-ray. You’re not on your own with the bottles any more.
Thank you, doctor. Thank you.

social.t: Brenda manages several opioid bottles alone and fears harming him. A written chart, a single named contact and the hospice line reduce that burden.
Her mother’s death in uncontrolled pain in 1998 shapes both her vow and her fear of morphine. Naming it lets you answer the real worry.

legal.t: Ronnie has capacity; check he is happy for his wife to speak for him and record it.

Tracey v Cambridge University Hospitals (2014): patients should be involved in DNACPR decisions unless this would cause physical or psychological harm. A letter that arrives without a prior conversation is worth checking with the hospice.
Morphine is a Schedule 2 controlled drug (oral solution at low strength is Schedule 5). Keep doses written and quantities reviewed; community pharmacy can help with disposal of unused stock.

professional.h: GMC Treatment and care towards the end of life (2010)
professional.t: Offer patients and families honest information, including about resuscitation, at a pace they can manage; support carers.
Contact the hospice team the same day and tell Brenda who is ringing whom and when; record the plan so out-of-hours services can see it.

community.t: Hospice community team and 24-hour advice line, district nursing, community pharmacy, Marie Curie and Macmillan for carer support, carer’s assessment from the local authority.

Back pain with leg weakness, numbness, or bladder or bowel change: suspected MSCC (NICE NG234)
Drowsiness, confusion, twitching (opioid toxicity); thirst, vomiting, constipation, confusion (hypercalcaemia)
psychosocial: Brenda’s capacity to manage the medicines alone
Her mother’s death and the morphine myth
The unopened resuscitation letter and what it means to both of them
ice: Idea: “The cancer is in his bones and the morphine has stopped working”
Concern: morphine “finishes them”; opening the letter makes it real
Expectation: written instructions, someone to see him, not being left alone

playbook.diagnosis: “The new pain in his thigh on standing may mean the bone has cracked where the cancer has weakened it. He needs an X-ray today. His top-up morphine is also too small for his regular dose.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “His slow morphine is the steady background, and the top-up is meant to cover the peaks. At the moment the top-up is too small to reach the peak — like trying to put out a bonfire with a cup of water.”

management.reflectIce: “You made a promise that he wouldn’t die in pain like your mum. Getting the dose right is how we keep that promise — morphine used properly doesn’t shorten life.”
management.psychosocial: Write the plan with her, give one number to ring, and offer to open the letter together at the visit.
sharedPlan: Same-day visit and X-ray of the right femur; no weight-bearing meanwhile
Hospice team contacted for titration; breakthrough dose within one-tenth to one-sixth of the 24-hour dose (BNF)
Bone-pain adjuncts and palliative radiotherapy considered; orthopaedic opinion if fracture; regular laxative
safetyNet: 999 if leg deformed, numb or useless, legs weak, or unable to pass urine
Ring the same day for drowsiness, confusion or twitching; GP call-back this evening

pitfalls.intro: This telephone station looks like a dosing question. It is failed by doctors who answer only the dose, miss the new mechanical pain, and never reach the fear or the envelope.

items.fail: Increasing the morphine by phone without asking why the pain changed.
items.why: New severe weight-bearing pain in a femur with metastases is a pathological fracture until imaged. Missing it is an unsafe plan.
items.fix: Ask what changed, advise no weight-bearing, and arrange same-day assessment and X-ray.

items.fail: Not noticing that the breakthrough dose is too small.
items.why: The recommended range is one-tenth to one-sixth of the 24-hour dose (6–10 mg on MST 30 mg twice daily). 5 mg is below it, which explains the poor response.
items.fix: Do the arithmetic aloud, agree the new dose with the hospice team, and put it in writing.

items.fail: Escalating opioids without a toxicity or MSCC screen.
items.why: Drowsiness, twitching or confusion change the plan; spinal metastases make MSCC a must-ask.
items.fix: Two quick questions each: sleepy or twitching? Legs weak, numb, bladder or bowel change?

items.fail: Answering “I’m frightened of doing something wrong” with a dose alone.
items.why: The fear contains the morphine myth and her mother’s death. Unaddressed, she will under-give.
items.fix: Explore the fear, then answer the myth honestly and link it to her story.

items.fail: Letting the mention of the letter pass, or telling her what it says.
items.why: The unopened envelope is the hidden agenda. Guessing its contents risks being wrong and dismissive.
items.fix: “What do you imagine is in it?” — then offer to open it together at the visit.

items.why: Non-specific safety-netting and no named follow-up are standard failing feedback.
items.fix: Named 999 and same-day triggers, a written chart at the visit, and a timed call-back.

avoid.instead: “The new pain on standing worries me — I want his thigh X-rayed today, and I’ll write down exactly what to give.”
avoid.why: Escalating opioids without assessing a possible fracture misses the diagnosis and leaves her with vague instructions.

avoid.dont: “Don’t worry about the morphine, it’s perfectly safe.”

SCA_MODELS.why: Explores the cue rather than just answering the dose question

SCA_MODELS.text: My mum died of cancer in 1998, screaming for help that never came. I promised myself Ronnie wouldn’t go like that. But I’ve heard it’s the morphine that finishes them at the end. So every time I give it, I think — am I helping him or…

Thank you for telling me — that’s a lot to be carrying on your own. I want to answer that properly. Morphine given in the right dose for pain does not shorten life. What it does is control the pain. What happened to your mum sounds like pain that wasn’t treated enough — and that is exactly what we’re going to prevent for Ronnie.
SCA_MODELS.why: Corrects the morphine myth honestly and links it to her story

SCA_MODELS.text: (pause) There’s a letter from the hospice we haven’t… we haven’t got round to opening. It’s about resuscitation.
Thank you for mentioning it — I’m glad you did. What do you imagine is in it?
SCA_MODELS.why: Picks up the sideways cue and explores it

SCA_MODELS.text: If we open it, it’s real, isn’t it? It’s on the mantelpiece. He pretends he can’t see it. I dust round it. What I really want is someone to see him — and tell me what I can give him without getting it wrong.

I’ll deal with the thigh first because it worries me most. Cancer in a thigh bone can weaken it, and pain like that on standing can mean the bone has cracked or is about to. There are good treatments if so — an operation to strengthen the bone, or a single session of radiotherapy — but he needs an X-ray today, and until then he mustn’t put weight through that leg.
SCA_MODELS.why: Explains suspected pathological fracture and names hopeful options

SCA_MODELS.text: Oh. I thought it was just the cancer getting worse.

It may be, but we check. The second thing is fixable today: his top-up dose is too small for the amount of slow-release morphine he’s on. For his dose the top-up should be larger — I’ll agree the exact amount with the hospice team this afternoon. And needing it five or six times a day tells us his background dose needs raising too.
SCA_MODELS.why: Explains the breakthrough mismatch and need for titration

SCA_MODELS.text: About the letter: I don’t know what it says, and I don’t want to guess on the phone. Letters like that are usually about making sure his wishes are known if his heart were to stop. It isn’t a decision made behind your backs, and it doesn’t change any other treatment. When I come, we can open it together, the three of us, if you both want to.
SCA_MODELS.why: Honest about uncertainty; offers to open it together

SCA_MODELS.text: I’d like that. I don’t think I could open it on my own.

So here’s the plan. I’ll visit this afternoon to examine his leg and check his kidney test results, and arrange an X-ray of the thigh today. I’ll ring the hospice team within the hour about his doses and about pain relief that helps bone pain in particular. Does that fit with your day?
SCA_MODELS.why: Same-day assessment, imaging and specialist input with clear timings

SCA_MODELS.text: Yes. We’re not going anywhere.

Until I arrive: help him with any moves — no standing on that leg. He can have his top-up now if he needs it. When I visit, I’ll write the new doses down with you, one sheet — what to give, how often, and a column to record the times. And keep the senna going every day; morphine and constipation go together.
SCA_MODELS.why: Handling advice, written plan and laxatives with opioid (NICE CG140)

SCA_MODELS.text: Written down. That’s what I need. I get muddled with all the bottles.
That’s why we’ll do it together. And Brenda — you’re doing a remarkable job. Ringing today was the right thing to do, not a sign you’re not coping.
SCA_MODELS.why: Supports the carer and reframes the call

SCA_MODELS.text: If his leg suddenly looks a different shape, can’t take any weight at all, or goes numb — or he can’t pass water or his legs go weak — ring 999 and tell them about the cancer in his bones. If he becomes very sleepy, muddled or starts twitching, ring the surgery or the hospice line straight away. Can you tell me back what you’ll do?
No standing on the leg. You’re coming this afternoon with the X-ray sorted. Leg looks wrong or numb or he can’t wee — 999. Sleepy or twitching — ring you. And we open the letter together.
Exactly. I’ll see you this afternoon, and I’ll ring you this evening once I’ve heard about the X-ray. You’re not on your own with the bottles any more.
Thank you, doctor. Thank you.

SCA_STEM.name: Ronald Hayes
pmh: Metastatic prostate cancer — bone metastases in spine, pelvis and both femurs
On the palliative care register; hospice community team involved
meds: Morphine sulfate modified-release (MST) 30 mg twice daily
Oramorph (morphine oral solution) 5 mg as required
SCA_STEM.recent: Hospice community team letter four days ago regarding resuscitation. Wife reports oramorph used 5–6 times daily for the last 3 days.
SCA_STEM.reason: Telephone call from his wife Brenda: “The pain’s got on top of him.”

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: NICE CG140 — Palliative care for adults: strong opioids · NICE NG234 — Spinal metastases and MSCC
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: New severe weight-bearing pain in a femur with metastases is a pathological fracture until imaged. His breakthrough dose is below the BNF range for his background morphine, and frequent PRN use means the regular dose needs review.

points.h: The change in pattern is the finding
points.t: Chronic bone-metastasis ache that suddenly becomes severe, focal and worse on weight-bearing (he “went white” standing from the commode) suggests an impending or actual pathological fracture. Same-day assessment and imaging; no weight-bearing on that leg meanwhile.

BNF: the breakthrough dose is usually one-tenth to one-sixth of the regular 24-hour dose, given every 2–4 hours as needed. MST 30 mg twice daily = 60 mg a day, so the PRN dose is 6–10 mg; 5 mg is below the range.

Regular need for several PRN doses a day means the background dose needs review: total the 24-hour opioid use and adjust with the palliative team, then recalculate the breakthrough dose. NICE CG140: prescribe laxatives regularly for everyone on strong opioids.
Ask about drowsiness, confusion, myoclonus (twitching), hallucinations and urine output; know his renal function. Opioid toxicity changes the plan.

points.h: Other red flags to screen by phone
points.t: Spinal metastases: new back pain, leg weakness, numbness, bladder or bowel change = suspected MSCC (NICE NG234), urgent same-day discussion with the acute oncology/MSCC service. Thirst, vomiting, constipation and confusion suggest hypercalcaemia.

Adjuncts for bone pain (an NSAID or dexamethasone, dose per BNF and hospice advice), single-fraction palliative radiotherapy for localised bone pain, and orthopaedic opinion on fixation if a fracture or impending fracture is found.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question; let Brenda describe the pain and her fear; checked Ronnie’s consent to discuss him.
Brenda as sole carer, her mother’s death in pain, the burden of managing bottles, their 43-year marriage.
“Frightened of doing something wrong” (dosing and the morphine myth); the unopened hospice letter.
Ideas (cancer in bones, morphine “stops working”); concerns (morphine shortens life, the letter); expectations (written plan, a visit, not being left alone).
Same-day visit and X-ray of the femur; renal function and calcium if toxicity or hypercalcaemia suspected.
Pathological fracture versus progression of bone pain; MSCC; opioid toxicity; hypercalcaemia.
Asked about deformity, leg weakness, numbness, bladder and bowel, drowsiness, twitching, thirst and vomiting.
Suspected pathological fracture of the right femur with uncontrolled bone pain and an inadequate breakthrough dose.
No weight-bearing; same-day imaging; hospice input on titration; breakthrough dose within the BNF range (one-tenth to one-sixth of the 24-hour dose); bone-pain adjuncts and radiotherapy considered.
Regular laxative with the opioid, renal function before escalation, carer support and the resuscitation letter.
999 triggers (deformed or numb leg, can’t pass urine, weak legs); same-day triggers (drowsiness, twitching); visit and evening call-back.

social.t: Brenda manages several opioid bottles alone and fears harming him. A written chart, a single named contact and the hospice line reduce that burden.
Her mother’s death in uncontrolled pain in 1998 shapes both her vow and her fear of morphine. Naming it lets you answer the real worry.

legal.t: Ronnie has capacity; check he is happy for his wife to speak for him and record it.

Tracey v Cambridge University Hospitals (2014): patients should be involved in DNACPR decisions unless this would cause physical or psychological harm. A letter that arrives without a prior conversation is worth checking with the hospice.
Morphine is a Schedule 2 controlled drug (oral solution at low strength is Schedule 5). Keep doses written and quantities reviewed; community pharmacy can help with disposal of unused stock.

professional.h: GMC Treatment and care towards the end of life (2010)
professional.t: Offer patients and families honest information, including about resuscitation, at a pace they can manage; support carers.
Contact the hospice team the same day and tell Brenda who is ringing whom and when; record the plan so out-of-hours services can see it.

community.t: Hospice community team and 24-hour advice line, district nursing, community pharmacy, Marie Curie and Macmillan for carer support, carer’s assessment from the local authority.

redFlags: New severe weight-bearing pain in a bone with metastases: suspected pathological fracture
Back pain with leg weakness, numbness, or bladder or bowel change: suspected MSCC (NICE NG234)
Drowsiness, confusion, twitching (opioid toxicity); thirst, vomiting, constipation, confusion (hypercalcaemia)
psychosocial: Brenda’s capacity to manage the medicines alone
Her mother’s death and the morphine myth
The unopened resuscitation letter and what it means to both of them
ice: Idea: “The cancer is in his bones and the morphine has stopped working”
Concern: morphine “finishes them”; opening the letter makes it real
Expectation: written instructions, someone to see him, not being left alone

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “The new pain in his thigh on standing may mean the bone has cracked where the cancer has weakened it. He needs an X-ray today. His top-up morphine is also too small for his regular dose.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “His slow morphine is the steady background, and the top-up is meant to cover the peaks. At the moment the top-up is too small to reach the peak — like trying to put out a bonfire with a cup of water.”

management.reflectIce: “You made a promise that he wouldn’t die in pain like your mum. Getting the dose right is how we keep that promise — morphine used properly doesn’t shorten life.”
management.psychosocial: Write the plan with her, give one number to ring, and offer to open the letter together at the visit.
sharedPlan: Same-day visit and X-ray of the right femur; no weight-bearing meanwhile
Hospice team contacted for titration; breakthrough dose within one-tenth to one-sixth of the 24-hour dose (BNF)
Bone-pain adjuncts and palliative radiotherapy considered; orthopaedic opinion if fracture; regular laxative
safetyNet: 999 if leg deformed, numb or useless, legs weak, or unable to pass urine
Ring the same day for drowsiness, confusion or twitching; GP call-back this evening

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This telephone station looks like a dosing question. It is failed by doctors who answer only the dose, miss the new mechanical pain, and never reach the fear or the envelope.

items.fail: Increasing the morphine by phone without asking why the pain changed.
items.why: New severe weight-bearing pain in a femur with metastases is a pathological fracture until imaged. Missing it is an unsafe plan.
items.fix: Ask what changed, advise no weight-bearing, and arrange same-day assessment and X-ray.

items.fail: Not noticing that the breakthrough dose is too small.
items.why: The recommended range is one-tenth to one-sixth of the 24-hour dose (6–10 mg on MST 30 mg twice daily). 5 mg is below it, which explains the poor response.
items.fix: Do the arithmetic aloud, agree the new dose with the hospice team, and put it in writing.

items.fail: Escalating opioids without a toxicity or MSCC screen.
items.why: Drowsiness, twitching or confusion change the plan; spinal metastases make MSCC a must-ask.
items.fix: Two quick questions each: sleepy or twitching? Legs weak, numb, bladder or bowel change?

items.fail: Answering “I’m frightened of doing something wrong” with a dose alone.
items.why: The fear contains the morphine myth and her mother’s death. Unaddressed, she will under-give.
items.fix: Explore the fear, then answer the myth honestly and link it to her story.

items.fail: Letting the mention of the letter pass, or telling her what it says.
items.why: The unopened envelope is the hidden agenda. Guessing its contents risks being wrong and dismissive.
items.fix: “What do you imagine is in it?” — then offer to open it together at the visit.

items.why: Non-specific safety-netting and no named follow-up are standard failing feedback.
items.fix: Named 999 and same-day triggers, a written chart at the visit, and a timed call-back.
